question.worked_solution:
The $2$nd row of the given matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So, using a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have   

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23}+1\cdot {C}_{24} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{2+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$  determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+2\cdot {C}_{12}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(6-2)-(-6-2) \\  & =-8-(-8) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+2\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+(2)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-6-2)+2(0-6) \\  & =-(-8)+2\cdot (-6) \\  & =8-12 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=-0+(-4)=-4.
$$
